Team UX project · Art discovery

Journey Through Design

Journey Through Design was my first time designing a product with a team. We built an art discovery app that connects design movements, artists, and their work.

Design focus Work within a shared design system and bring usability observations back to the team.

PROJECT CONTEXT

Project and approach

One person might come to learn about a period. Someone else might already know the name of an artist. Our team designed for both kinds of exploration, starting with low-fidelity wireframes, refining the screens at mid fidelity, and building a full interactive prototype in Figma.

I contributed to the design and ran usability testing as part of GIT 540 Team 9. The screens and design system are shared team work. The session notes shown here are from testing I conducted.

01 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Design for browsing and searching

We used a timeline for people who wanted to explore a period and search for people who had a name or subject in mind. Filters narrowed the collection. Since those routes could lead to the same artist or artwork, we also had to consider where someone would expect to go when they went back.

02 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Notice where people hesitate

In a mid-fidelity test I ran, a participant completed the first task and still said “going back” was confusing. My notes also captured uncertainty around filters. Those moments gave us concrete things to review, including where to put return links and how to show that a filter had been applied.

03 / DESIGN DECISIONS

Keep the screens consistent as a team

We used shared type, color, navigation, and controls so the timeline, search, and detail pages would feel related as the prototype came together. In later sessions, I documented people successfully navigating the gallery, search, timeline filters, and artwork. I’d still revisit the earlier points of confusion in another round of testing.

REFLECTION

What I learned and what I’d test next

Working with other designers taught me the value of shared patterns, especially when several screens have to feel like one experience. Testing taught me to look for hesitation even when someone finished a task. I’d retest the same browsing tasks with new participants and watch whether they can return to the previous view and tell which filters are active without help.
